When the Conference kicked off in August 1979, twenty clubs set out to prove that football beyond the Football League could be professional, credible, and worth watching. Altrincham was there from the start — and they're still here.

It's easy to overlook what that means. In forty-five years, the National League has seen clubs fold, reform, vanish into the lower reaches of the pyramid, or step away from the game entirely. Altrincham never blinked. They've been a fixture in the top tier of non-league football for nearly half a century, a quiet constant in an English football landscape that's been remade three times over.

The 1979-80 season was an experiment. The twenty founding members — Altrincham among them — were betting yes. They were right.

What's striking about Altrincham's longevity is that it's never been flashy. They've had their moments: promotion pushes, cup runs, the occasional player who caught a bigger club's eye. But they've built something more durable than glory — a club rooted in the community, sustainable, run with a steady hand. That's harder than it sounds. It's the difference between a club that survives and a club that lasts.

In 1979, non-league football carried a whiff of the makeshift. Teams played in front of small crowds, on patchy pitches, in grounds that had seen better days. The idea that this could be a genuine alternative to the Football League seemed optimistic at best. Forty-five years later, the National League is a professional competition, televised, competitive, and recognised as a legitimate stepping stone to the Football League. They've built the infrastructure, nurtured the talent, kept the lights on through the lean years, and stayed true to what a football club is supposed to be: a focal point for a community, a reason to gather, a place where something that matters happens on a Saturday afternoon.

Not every founding member of 1979 can say that. Altrincham can.
